The second holds that social and economic inequalities are permissible only if, first, they attach to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity, and second, they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged, the difference principle. Inequalities are justified, in other words, only when they help those at the bottom, for example by giving productive people incentives that generate resources which, through taxation and provision, improve the position of the worst-off. Rawls's theory is a form of liberal egalitarianism, combining strong personal liberties with a demanding commitment to distributive fairness, and it dominated debate for decades. The most powerful libertarian reply came from Robert Nozick, whose 1974 Anarchy, State, and Utopia defends a minimal state limited to protecting people against force, theft, and fraud and to enforcing contracts, anything more, he argued, violates rights. Nozick advanced an entitlement theory of justice: a distribution is just if it arose from just original acquisition and just voluntary transfers, regardless of the resulting pattern. He objected that theories aiming at a particular pattern of distribution, like Rawls's, must continually interfere with people's free choices to maintain it, illustrating with the example of a beloved athlete whom fans freely pay, producing inequality that redistribution could correct only by forbidding voluntary exchanges; taxation of earnings, he provocatively claimed, is on a par with forced labor. Between and beyond these poles lie other views. Utilitarians hold that the just distribution is the one that maximizes total welfare. Luck egalitarians argue that inequalities stemming from unchosen bad luck are unjust while those flowing from genuine choice are not. Others, following Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum, shift the focus from goods or welfare to capabilities, what people are actually able to do and to be, arguing that justice requires securing a threshold of central human capabilities for all. The debate remains open, but Rawls and Nozick defined its terms, forcing every serious position to say what it distributes, on what principle, and at what cost to liberty.

sections.heading: Equality and Its Varieties
sections.body: The idea that human beings are in some sense equal is among the most powerful in modern politics, animating movements against slavery, aristocracy, colonial rule, and the subordination of women, yet the idea is more complex than it appears, because people plainly differ in strength, talent, and circumstance, and few believe every difference should be erased. Political philosophy therefore distinguishes the respects in which equality is claimed. At the deepest level lies basic moral equality, the claim that all persons have equal fundamental worth and are owed equal concern and respect, a claim that grounds much of modern ethics though its own justification, whether it rests on shared rationality, capacity for suffering, being made in a divine image, or simply a moral commitment, is debated. From basic equality flow more specific ideals. Legal and political equality demand that all be equal before the law and enjoy equal political rights, one person, one vote, a hard-won achievement extended only gradually to the propertyless, to women, and to racial minorities. Equality of opportunity holds that positions and advantages should be open to all on the basis of relevant qualifications rather than birth or connections; in its formal version it merely bars explicit discrimination, while a fair or substantive version, defended by Rawls, requires that people with similar talents and motivation have similar prospects regardless of their starting social position, which implies attending to the family and educational circumstances that shape early life. Distributive equality concerns the shares of income, wealth, and resources people hold, and here disagreement is sharpest. Strict egalitarians favor equal shares; but critics ask why equality itself should matter, raising the leveling-down objection, that making the better-off worse off, benefiting no one, seems perverse if equality is the only value. In response, some argue that what we should care about is not equality as such but priority, giving greater weight to improving the lot of the worse-off, or sufficiency, ensuring everyone has enough for a decent life, rather than equal amounts. A further influential distinction concerns responsibility: luck egalitarians hold that it is unjust for people to be worse off through no fault of their own, through the natural lottery of talents or the social lottery of birth, but not unjust when disadvantage results from their own free and informed choices, so justice should neutralize brute luck while allowing the consequences of choice. This position faces the hard objection that drawing the line between luck and choice is deeply difficult and that a harsh version might abandon those whose bad choices leave them destitute. Relational egalitarians, such as Elizabeth Anderson, reframe the whole debate, arguing that equality is fundamentally about social relationships, about people standing as equals free from domination, hierarchy, and contempt, rather than about the arithmetic of distributions. On this view the point of equality is to end oppression and to create a community of equals, and material distribution matters chiefly insofar as it serves or undermines that standing. These varieties of equality often pull in different directions, and clarifying which equality one means is essential to any coherent argument about justice.

sections.heading: Democracy: Justifications and Discontents
sections.body: Democracy, rule by the people, is today so widely praised that its justification can seem obvious, yet philosophers have long asked why the many should rule and whether their rule is wise or just. The word comes from the Greek for people and power, and the ancient Athenian democracy of the fifth and fourth centuries BCE, in which citizens governed directly through assembly, lot, and rotation, was as often criticized as admired. Plato condemned it as the rule of the ignorant, likening the state to a ship whose sailors, knowing nothing of navigation, seize the helm from the one who does. This challenge, that political decisions require knowledge most citizens lack, still troubles democratic theory. Several distinct justifications for democracy answer it. Instrumental justifications hold that democracy produces better outcomes than the alternatives: it protects citizens' interests because rulers who must face election cannot easily ignore the governed, as Amartya Sen observed that no substantial famine has occurred in a functioning democracy with a free press; and it may harness dispersed knowledge, the diverse information and judgment of many minds, better than any elite, a thought formalized in results suggesting that under certain conditions large groups of modestly reliable voters are collectively very likely to reach correct decisions. Intrinsic or procedural justifications hold that democracy is valuable in itself because it treats citizens as free and equal, giving each an equal say in the decisions that bind all, so that democratic authority expresses respect for persons and public equality regardless of the quality of its outcomes. Deliberative democrats, such as Jürgen Habermas and Joshua Cohen, argue that democracy's legitimacy rests not merely on counting votes but on the quality of public reasoning that precedes them, on collective decisions being justified through open deliberation among equals who offer reasons others can accept. Against these justifications stand persistent discontents. The problem of the tyranny of the majority, emphasized by Alexis de Tocqueville and Mill, warns that a majority may oppress minorities, motivating constitutional limits and protected rights that democracy itself may not override. The problem of voter ignorance and irrationality, pressed by recent critics who advocate forms of epistocracy, rule weighted toward the more informed, questions whether citizens know enough to govern well. The problem of scale and self-interest, and the influence of concentrated wealth over ostensibly equal politics, raises doubts about whether modern representative democracies truly realize political equality. Defenders reply that no feasible alternative better combines legitimacy, accountability, and the protection of interests, and that the remedy for democracy's defects is usually more and better democracy, wider participation, stronger deliberation, fairer institutions, rather than its abandonment. The debate matters because most people now accept democracy's legitimacy without examining its grounds, and understanding those grounds clarifies both what we may demand of democratic institutions and where their authority reaches its limits.

sections.heading: Rights, Law, and the Rule of Law
sections.body: The language of rights pervades modern political and moral life, from constitutional bills of rights to international declarations, and clarifying what rights are and where they come from is a central task of political philosophy. A right is, roughly, a justified claim that others, or the state, treat one in certain ways, and rights are commonly distinguished by their force and function. The philosopher Wesley Hohfeld analyzed rights into more precise relations, distinguishing a claim-right, which correlates with a duty in another, from a liberty, a power, and an immunity, showing that loose talk of rights conceals several different relations. A further distinction separates negative rights, which require others merely to refrain from interfering, such as rights against assault or censorship, from positive rights, which require others to provide something, such as rights to education or health care, a distinction that bears on how demanding and how feasible various rights are. The deepest debate concerns the foundation of rights. Natural-rights theorists, in the tradition of Locke, hold that certain rights belong to persons by virtue of their nature or humanity, independent of any legal recognition, and are discoverable by reason; the American Declaration's appeal to unalienable rights expresses this view. Jeremy Bentham scorned such talk, calling natural rights nonsense upon stilts, and argued that rights are the creations of law, useful fictions justified by their contribution to general welfare; on this legal-positivist and utilitarian view, to have a right is to be the intended beneficiary of a legally imposed duty. Between these poles, contemporary theorists ground rights in the protection of fundamental human interests weighty enough to hold others under duties, as Joseph Raz argues, or in the requirements of treating persons as ends in themselves, following Kant. Ronald Dworkin influentially described rights as trumps that individuals hold against the majority, protections that cannot be overridden merely because doing so would increase overall welfare, capturing the idea that rights shield the individual from being sacrificed for the collective. Rights connect intimately to law and to the ideal of the rule of law, the principle that people should be governed by known, general, stable, publicly promulgated rules applied impartially, rather than by the arbitrary will of officials. The rule of law demands that laws be clear, prospective, consistent, and enforced through fair procedures, and that even the highest officials be subject to the law, an ideal captured in the phrase a government of laws, not of men. Legal philosophers debate whether law is conceptually connected to morality: natural-law theorists, from Aquinas to Lon Fuller and John Finnis, hold that genuine law must meet moral standards, so that a grossly unjust command is not truly law, while legal positivists, from Bentham and John Austin to H. L. A. Hart, insist that the existence of law is one thing and its merit another, so that even wicked laws are laws, though they may not deserve obedience. This dispute has practical weight, bearing on how citizens and officials should respond to unjust legal orders and on the moral significance of legality itself.

sections.heading: Property, Markets, and Economic Justice
sections.body: Few questions divide political philosophies more sharply than the justification and limits of private property and the market economy. Property is not a simple relation between a person and a thing but a bundle of socially recognized rights, to use, to exclude others, to transfer, to derive income, defined and enforced by law, so that what counts as property and what an owner may do with it are always partly political decisions. The classic defense of private property comes from Locke, who argued that although the earth was originally given to humanity in common, a person acquires property by mixing his labor with unowned resources, making them his, provided, in his famous proviso, that enough and as good is left for others. This labor theory of appropriation grounds property in individual effort and has powerfully shaped liberal and libertarian thought, though critics note that the proviso is hard to satisfy once resources are scarce and that much property derives not from one's own labor but from inheritance, luck, and force. Utilitarian defenders, such as Hume and later economists, justify property and markets not by natural right but by their consequences: secure property rights and free exchange coordinate the plans of millions, provide incentives to produce and innovate, and, as Adam Smith argued, channel self-interest toward outcomes that benefit society, so that a butcher and baker serve us not from benevolence but from regard to their own interest. Markets are prized for their efficiency and for the freedom they give people to trade and to pursue their own ends. Yet the market has powerful critics. Karl Marx argued that under capitalism the worker, owning no means of production, must sell his labor to those who do, and is exploited because he produces more value than he is paid, the surplus appropriated by the owner; he saw private property in the means of production as the root of class domination and alienation, to be overcome by collective ownership. Short of Marxism, social-democratic and egalitarian liberals accept markets but insist they be embedded in institutions that correct their failures and injustices: markets can generate great inequalities, leave the vulnerable destitute, produce harms like pollution that fall on third parties, and undersupply public goods, so justice requires redistribution through taxation, provision of education, health care, and social insurance, and regulation of the terms of exchange. Debates over economic justice thus turn on several deep disagreements: whether the distribution produced by voluntary market transactions is just simply because it arose from free choices, as Nozick held, or whether it must be judged by its pattern and its effect on the worst-off, as Rawls held; whether there are goods, such as votes, bodily organs, or basic necessities, that should not be for sale at all, as Michael Sandel and others argue in worrying about the moral limits of markets; and whether the workplace itself should be subject to democratic norms rather than treated as the owner's private domain. How a society answers these questions shapes its economy and the life prospects of its members, making economic justice one of the subject's most consequential arenas.

sections.heading: Community, Culture, and Identity
sections.body: Much of modern political philosophy, especially in the liberal tradition, centers on the individual as the bearer of rights and the unit of justice, but a series of powerful critiques has insisted that this focus is incomplete, that human beings are constituted by their communities, cultures, and identities, and that political theory must reckon with belonging as well as with individual freedom. The communitarian critics of the 1980s, including Michael Sandel, Charles Taylor, Alasdair MacIntyre, and Michael Walzer, challenged the liberal picture, particularly Rawls's, of the self as an abstract chooser prior to its ends. They argued that we are, in Sandel's phrase, encumbered selves, partly defined by attachments we did not choose, to family, nation, faith, and tradition, and that the goods and virtues by which we live make sense only within particular communities and their shared understandings. On this view justice cannot be derived from a standpoint abstracted from all social membership, as the veil of ignorance seems to attempt, but must draw on the meanings a community attaches to its goods; Walzer accordingly argued for complex equality, in which different social goods, money, office, honor, health care, are distributed by different principles internal to their distinct spheres, with injustice arising when dominance in one sphere, such as wealth, is used to command goods in others. Liberals replied that they need not deny the importance of community, only insist that individuals retain the freedom to question and revise their inherited ends, and that a just framework must remain neutral among the many conceptions of the good life that citizens hold. A related set of questions concerns cultural diversity within states. Multiculturalists such as Will Kymlicka argue that because a secure cultural context provides the meaningful options from which individuals choose, justice may require special group-differentiated rights or accommodations for minority cultures, so that neutrality among cultures is not enough and fair treatment may demand active support. Critics worry that group rights can entrench internal hierarchies and trap vulnerable members, especially women, within oppressive traditions, raising the tension Susan Okin highlighted between multiculturalism and feminism. Feminist political philosophy has itself transformed the field by exposing how the supposedly universal and gender-neutral categories of traditional theory often reflected a male standpoint and confined justice to the public sphere while leaving the family, where much of women's subordination occurs, unexamined; the slogan that the personal is political captures the insistence that relations within the household, the division of domestic labor, and the norms of care are matters of justice, not of private nature. Theorists of care, following Carol Gilligan and Joan Tronto, further argue that an ethics centered on autonomous rights-bearers neglects the dependence and caregiving that structure every human life, and that a just society must value and fairly share the work of care. Together these currents enrich political philosophy by insisting that abstract individuals do not exhaust the moral reality of politics, and that community, culture, gender, and care shape both the identities of citizens and the demands of justice.

sections.heading: Power, Ideology, and the Radical Critique
sections.body: Alongside the tradition that asks how the state should be justly ordered runs a more radical current that asks whether the very categories of mainstream political philosophy, rights, consent, the neutral state, conceal and legitimate domination. Its greatest figure is Karl Marx, who inverted the usual approach. Rather than asking what justice ideally requires, he sought to explain politics by its material foundations, arguing that in every epoch the ruling ideas are the ideas of the ruling class, and that the state, law, and prevailing morality function as a superstructure serving the interests of those who control the means of production. On this view the liberal celebration of formal equality and freedom masks substantive class exploitation: the worker is formally free to sell his labor but materially compelled to do so on terms set by owners, and rights that look universal chiefly protect property. Marx introduced the concept of ideology, systematically distorted thought that presents the particular interests of the dominant as the universal interest of all and makes an unjust order appear natural and inevitable; the task of critique is to unmask this and to change the world, not merely interpret it. The tradition of critical theory that followed, associated with the Frankfurt School and thinkers such as Theodor Adorno, Max Horkheimer, and later Jürgen Habermas, extended the analysis of domination beyond the economic to culture, mass communication, and the subtle ways modern rationality can become an instrument of control, while Habermas turned toward the emancipatory potential of undistorted communication and rational discourse. A different and highly influential analysis of power came from Michel Foucault, who argued that power is not merely a possession of the state exercised from above through law and prohibition, but is dispersed throughout society, productive as well as repressive, operating through institutions, prisons, clinics, schools, and through the very forms of knowledge that define what is normal, healthy, or sane. Modern power, he argued, works through discipline and surveillance, shaping bodies and souls, and produces the subjects it governs; his phrase power-knowledge captures the claim that regimes of power and bodies of knowledge are inseparable, each sustaining the other. Such analyses caution that emancipation is never simply a matter of removing external constraints, because power constitutes our very desires and self-understandings. Antonio Gramsci added the concept of hegemony, the way a dominant class secures rule not only by coercion but by winning consent, leadership over the culture and common sense of a society, so that domination is sustained through belief as much as force. These radical critiques do not offer a tidy alternative blueprint, and they are themselves criticized, for economic reductionism in Marx's case, for a corrosive skepticism that seems to leave no ground for judgment in Foucault's, but they perform an indispensable function. They compel political philosophy to ask whose interests its concepts serve, to notice the forms of domination that formal freedom and equality can hide, and to remain alert to the gap between the ideals a society proclaims and the power relations it actually sustains.

sections.heading: Global Justice and Where the Questions Lead
sections.body: Traditional political philosophy took the self-contained nation-state as the arena of justice, asking how the members of a single society should order their common life; but in a world of vast international inequality, global markets, migration, and shared threats such as climate change, philosophers increasingly ask whether the principles of justice reach across borders, and if so how far. The debate divides broadly into cosmopolitans and their critics. Cosmopolitans, such as Peter Singer, Thomas Pogge, and Charles Beitz, argue that the moral equality of all persons cannot stop at national boundaries, which are morally arbitrary lines that no one chose; if we owe justice to fellow citizens, we owe something to distant strangers too. Singer argued, from the premise that we ought to prevent great suffering when we can do so at modest cost, that affluent individuals have strong duties to aid the global poor, comparing ignoring distant famine to walking past a drowning child. Pogge went further, contending that the wealthy nations are not merely failing to help but are actively implicated in harming the poor by imposing an unjust global economic order that perpetuates poverty, so that reform is a matter of justice, not charity. Against strong cosmopolitanism, statists and liberal nationalists, including a cautious late position of Rawls himself in The Law of Peoples, argue that the demanding principles of distributive justice apply within a state because citizens share coercive institutions and a cooperative scheme that generate special obligations, and that beyond the state the duties are real but weaker, duties of humanitarian assistance and fair dealing rather than global egalitarian redistribution. This dispute bears directly on urgent questions: the ethics of immigration and whether states may exclude would-be members; the justice of the global trade, finance, and intellectual-property regimes; the responsibilities of rich and poor nations for climate change and its burdens; and the legitimacy of humanitarian intervention across sovereign borders. These global questions bring the survey full circle, for they are new forms of the oldest questions, about authority, its scope and limits, about liberty, whose and against whom, about justice in distribution, now among nations and generations, about equality, of all human beings, and about power, exercised globally and often unaccountably. Political philosophy offers no final answers to any of them, and honest students of the subject learn to live with reasonable, persistent disagreement among thoughtful people. But the discipline is not therefore fruitless. It clarifies what is at stake, exposes the assumptions buried in political rhetoric, tests arguments against objections, and cultivates the capacity to reason about power and justice rather than merely to feel or assert. In a democracy whose citizens must ultimately judge these matters, that capacity is not a luxury but a civic necessity, and the great questions, unresolved for millennia, remain unavoidable because human beings must go on living together and deciding, again and again, on what terms.

guides.title: What Political Science Studies
guides.summary: A comprehensive introduction to political science: how the discipline studies power, the state, and collective decision-making, spanning political theory, comparative politics, democracy and authoritarianism, elections and behavior, international relations, and public policy, along with its methods, debates, and pitfalls.

sections.heading: Defining the Discipline: Power, Authority, and the State
sections.body:
Political science is the systematic study of politics: of power, and of how human beings organize collective life, make binding decisions, resolve conflicts, and govern themselves. Politics arises wherever people must decide things together and disagree about what to do; it is, in Harold Lasswell's durable phrase, the study of who gets what, when, and how. Because such questions touch every society, the discipline is ancient in its subject matter even though its modern, self-conscious form dates only to the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

At the center of the field sit a few core concepts. Power is the capacity to get others to do what they otherwise would not, whether by force, by inducement, or by shaping their very preferences. Authority is power widely accepted as rightful, so that people obey not merely from fear but from a sense of obligation. Legitimacy is the belief that a ruler or institution has the right to command; the sociologist Max Weber distinguished three of its bases, traditional (inherited custom), charismatic (the extraordinary appeal of a leader), and rational-legal (impersonal rules and offices), the last being the foundation of the modern state.

The state itself is the discipline's principal object. Following Weber, a state is an organization that successfully claims a monopoly on the legitimate use of physical force within a defined territory. A state possesses a population, a bounded territory, a government, and sovereignty, the recognized supreme authority to make and enforce law at home and to act independently abroad. The state must be distinguished from the government, which is the particular set of people and offices currently exercising state authority and which changes while the state endures, and from the nation, a community bound by shared identity that may or may not coincide with a state.

Political science studies these phenomena at every scale: the behavior of individual voters and leaders, the design of constitutions and legislatures, the character of whole regimes, and the interactions of states in the international arena. It overlaps with, but is distinct from, its sister disciplines. It shares economics' interest in incentives and choice, sociology's interest in groups and institutions, history's interest in change over time, philosophy's interest in justice, and law's interest in rules, yet it is unified by its focus on the acquisition, exercise, distribution, and limitation of political power.

Two ambitions run through all of this. The empirical ambition is to describe and explain how politics actually works, why some states are stable and others collapse, why people vote as they do, when wars occur. The normative ambition is to evaluate how politics ought to work, what makes authority just, what citizens owe one another, how power should be constrained. Holding both ambitions together, without collapsing one into the other, gives political science its distinctive character.

sections.heading: The Discipline's Methods and Subfields
sections.body:
Political science pursues its questions with a range of methods and organizes itself into recognizable subfields, and understanding this internal map clarifies what the discipline can and cannot deliver. Broadly, its approaches fall into three families. Empirical or positive analysis seeks to describe and explain the political world as it is, using observation and evidence to test claims about cause and effect. Normative or political theory reasons about how the political world ought to be, clarifying and defending values such as liberty, equality, and justice. Formal analysis builds mathematical models, drawn largely from game theory and economics, to derive the logical consequences of assumptions about rational actors. These are complementary rather than rival; a full account of an election, for instance, may draw on all three.

The empirical side has grown increasingly rigorous. Quantitative work gathers large datasets, on votes, wars, economic indicators, or survey responses, and uses statistical methods to look for patterns and estimate relationships, always mindful that correlation is not causation. Qualitative work relies on close case studies, comparative history, interviews, and careful interpretation to understand particular events and processes in depth. Increasingly, scholars use experiments, including randomized field experiments, to isolate causes. Each method has strengths and blind spots: statistics can generalize but may miss context, case studies illuminate mechanisms but may not generalize, and no method escapes the problem that political outcomes have many tangled causes and cannot be run over again under controlled conditions.

By convention the discipline divides into several major subfields. Political theory studies the great normative questions and the history of political thought. Comparative politics examines the internal politics of countries, comparing regimes, institutions, parties, and behavior across cases to build general explanations. International relations studies interactions among states and other global actors: war and peace, diplomacy, trade, and international organizations. Public administration and public policy study how governments implement decisions and how policies are designed, adopted, and evaluated. Many programs add political economy, which analyzes the entanglement of markets and states, and methodology itself as a field of study.

The discipline's scientific status is genuinely and reasonably debated. Its subject, human beings who anticipate, react, and change, does not sit still like the objects of physics, and its concepts, such as power or democracy, are contested and value-laden. Predictions are probabilistic at best; the fall of the Soviet Union and the outcomes of many elections surprised most experts. Honest practitioners therefore claim explanation of tendencies and mechanisms rather than laws, and they treat their theories as fallible tools. What makes the enterprise scientific is not certainty but its commitment to explicit reasoning, evidence, and the possibility of being proven wrong, an attitude that separates it from mere opinion about politics.

sections.heading: Political Theory: The Normative Tradition
sections.body:
Political theory, the oldest branch of the discipline, asks how political life ought to be arranged and on what grounds anyone may rightfully hold power over anyone else. It is normative rather than descriptive, reasoning about justice, liberty, equality, authority, and the good society, and it proceeds through argument and the critical reading of a long canon of thinkers. Its questions are perennial because they cannot be settled by data alone: no measurement tells us whether a law is just.

The tradition begins in ancient Greece. Plato's Republic (c. 380 BCE) argued that the just state, like the just soul, is one in which each part performs its proper role, and it proposed rule by philosopher-guardians who know the good, a frank rejection of democracy. His student Aristotle, in the Politics, took a more empirical turn, classifying constitutions by who rules and in whose interest, and famously calling the human being a political animal, naturally suited to life in a polis. These works framed debates, about the best regime, the rule of law, and the ends of political community, that recur ever after.

Early modern theory reconceived authority through the idea of a social contract: legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed, imagined as an agreement to leave a pre-political state of nature. Thomas Hobbes, in Leviathan (1651), argued that without a common power life would be a war of all against all, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short, so rational individuals surrender their freedom to an absolute sovereign for security. John Locke, in the Second Treatise (1689), countered that people possess natural rights to life, liberty, and property, that government exists to protect them, and that a government violating this trust may rightfully be resisted, ideas that shaped the American and later revolutions. Jean-Jacques Rousseau located legitimacy in the general will of a self-governing people.

The nineteenth century deepened the argument. Utilitarians such as Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill judged institutions by whether they produced the greatest happiness of the greatest number, while Mill's On Liberty (1859) mounted a classic defense of individual freedom against social and governmental tyranny. Karl Marx offered a searching critique of capitalism and of the state as an instrument of class domination, predicting its transformation.

Twentieth-century theory revived after mid-century with John Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971), which asked what principles people would choose for society from behind a veil of ignorance, not knowing their own place in it, and derived principles protecting basic liberties and permitting inequalities only when they benefit the least advantaged. Robert Nozick's libertarian reply, communitarian and feminist critiques, and theories of democracy and multiculturalism continue the conversation, ensuring that the normative core of political science remains alive and contested.

sections.heading: Comparative Politics: Regimes and Institutions
sections.body:
Comparative politics is the empirical study of the internal political life of countries, pursued by comparing many cases to find what explains political outcomes. Its guiding logic is that we learn what causes stability, democracy, revolution, or growth only by contrasting places where these occur with places where they do not. If every prosperous democracy shares a feature that struggling states lack, that feature becomes a candidate explanation, to be tested against further cases and rival accounts.

A first task is classifying regimes, the fundamental rules by which a country is governed. The broadest division separates democracies, in which rulers are chosen through free and fair competitive elections and are constrained by law and rights, from authoritarian regimes, in which power is not subject to genuine electoral accountability. Between these lie hybrid regimes, sometimes called competitive authoritarian, which hold elections that are real enough to matter but tilted enough that the incumbent rarely loses. Scholars refine these categories further, distinguishing, for instance, personalist, military, one-party, and monarchical forms of authoritarian rule, because how a dictatorship is organized affects how it behaves and how it might fall.

Comparative politics pays close attention to institutions, the formal and informal rules that structure political behavior, on the premise that institutions shape incentives and outcomes. A central contrast is between presidential systems, such as that of the United States, in which a separately elected president heads the executive for a fixed term, and parliamentary systems, such as that of the United Kingdom, in which the executive emerges from and depends on the confidence of the legislature and can fall between scheduled elections. Semi-presidential systems, as in France, combine a directly elected president with a prime minister answerable to parliament. Federalism, which divides authority between national and regional governments, contrasts with unitary systems that concentrate it. These design choices influence how easily governments can act, how power is checked, and how conflict is managed.

Beyond regime type and institutional design, the field investigates recurring big questions. Why do some countries democratize and others not, and once democratic, why do some backslide? Modernization theory once linked democracy to economic development, an association that holds statistically but with important exceptions. What explains political order versus state failure, ethnic conflict, or revolution? Why do some states deliver growth and public services while others are captured by narrow elites?

Comparativists differ over method. Some pursue large-N statistical studies across dozens or hundreds of countries to establish general patterns; others conduct in-depth case studies or paired comparisons to trace exactly how outcomes come about. The most persuasive work often combines them, using broad correlations to identify tendencies and detailed cases to reveal the mechanisms behind them, always alert that similar-looking outcomes may spring from very different causes in different settings.

sections.heading: The State, Sovereignty, and Legitimacy
sections.body:
Although introduced earlier, the state deserves sustained attention because it is the container within which most politics occurs and the actor whose rise, forms, and limits political science works hardest to explain. The modern state is a historically specific invention. For most of human history people lived under tribes, empires, city-states, and feudal arrangements in which authority was overlapping and personal. The consolidated territorial state, with clear borders, a single supreme authority, and a professional administration, emerged in Europe over several centuries and is conventionally dated to the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, which is taken to mark the principle that each state is sovereign within its own territory and equal to others.

Sovereignty is the state's defining attribute, and it has two faces. Internal sovereignty is supreme authority within the territory: the state makes the ultimate law and no other body may override it. External sovereignty is independence from outside control and recognition as an equal member of the international system. In practice sovereignty is never absolute; states are constrained by their own constitutions, by domestic power holders, and by treaties, alliances, markets, and international bodies. Globalization has led some to argue that sovereignty is eroding, while others reply that states remain the decisive units of world politics, adapting rather than dissolving.

The state's core functions help explain why it endures. It provides security against external threat and internal disorder; it makes and enforces law and adjudicates disputes; it extracts revenue through taxation and manages a currency; it delivers public goods and, in modern welfare states, extensive services in health, education, and social insurance. Charles Tilly's memorable thesis that war made the state and the state made war captures how the need to fight and finance wars drove rulers to build the tax systems and bureaucracies that became the modern state's backbone.

Legitimacy is what allows a state to perform these functions without ruling by force alone. A regime that most people regard as rightful can govern cheaply, since citizens comply voluntarily; a regime that has lost legitimacy must spend ever more on coercion and remains brittle. States cultivate legitimacy through effective performance, through fair procedures and consent, through national identity and shared symbols, and through ideology. When legitimacy fails and coercion falters, states weaken.

At the extreme, states fail. A failed or fragile state cannot maintain its monopoly on force, provide basic order, or deliver services across its territory, producing insecurity that spills across borders. Studying why states form, strengthen, weaken, and collapse, from the fiscal-military states of early modern Europe to fragile states today, is one of the discipline's central and most consequential projects, bearing directly on war, development, and human welfare.

sections.heading: Democracy: Forms, Measures, and Debates
sections.body:
Democracy, from the Greek for rule by the people, is government in which political authority ultimately rests with the citizenry, exercised through their participation in choosing and constraining those who govern. It is both an ideal and a set of institutions, and political science studies the gap between the two. The word covers a range of arrangements, so the first task is to be precise about what is meant.

A minimal, procedural definition, associated with Joseph Schumpeter, treats democracy as a method: a system in which leaders acquire power through a competitive struggle for the people's vote. On this view the essential test is regular, free, and fair elections in which incumbents can actually lose. Robert Dahl expanded the account into what he called polyarchy, arguing that meaningful democracy requires not only elections but a bundle of supporting conditions: freedom of expression and the press, freedom to form and join organizations, broad suffrage, the right to run for office, alternative sources of information, and institutions that make policy depend on votes. Richer, substantive definitions add protection of minority rights, the rule of law, and even social and economic equality, on the ground that formal voting rights mean little without the capacity to use them.

Democracies also differ in form. Direct democracy, in which citizens themselves decide policy, as in ancient Athens or in modern referendums, contrasts with representative democracy, the normal modern arrangement in which citizens elect officials to decide on their behalf. Within representative democracy, majoritarian models concentrate power to produce decisive government answerable to the majority, while consensus models disperse power to include many groups in decision-making, a contrast Arend Lijphart analyzed in depth. Liberal democracy combines majority rule with entrenched individual rights and limits on power, whereas illiberal or majoritarian systems may hold elections while eroding those constraints.

Because democracy is contested, scholars have built indices to measure it, such as Freedom House ratings, the Polity project, and the Varieties of Democracy dataset, each operationalizing the concept differently and each imperfect. These tools allow the study of trends, including recent concern about democratic backsliding, the gradual weakening of checks, media freedom, and fair competition by elected leaders themselves, which typically proceeds through legal steps rather than dramatic coups.

Enduring debates surround democracy's value and viability. Does it require prior economic development, a supportive civic culture, or particular institutions to survive? Are citizens informed enough for self-government, given evidence of widespread political ignorance, or does democracy aggregate dispersed knowledge well enough despite this? Is majority rule a threat to minorities that rights must restrain? Political science does not resolve whether democracy is best, a normative question, but it has learned a great deal about the conditions under which it emerges, thrives, and decays.

sections.heading: Authoritarianism and Hybrid Regimes
sections.body:
Most of human history, and much of the present world, has been governed without democracy, so understanding authoritarian rule is not a marginal topic but a central one. An authoritarian regime is one in which political power is not genuinely accountable to citizens through free and fair elections, and in which opposition, media, and civil society are constrained. Far from being all alike, such regimes vary enormously, and their internal organization shapes how they behave, how repressive they are, how they handle succession, and how they end.

Scholars distinguish several types. In a one-party regime, a single ruling party monopolizes politics and organizes elite careers and mass mobilization, as in the Soviet Union or China. In a military regime, the armed forces rule directly, typically after a coup, and often present themselves as temporary guardians. In a personalist regime, power is concentrated in a single leader who dominates the party, army, and state and rules through loyalty and patronage rather than institutions. Absolute monarchies persist in a few states. These types are ideal cases; real regimes often blend them, and how power is arranged affects their stability, since personalist rulers, for instance, tend to produce more erratic policy and messier collapses than institutionalized parties.

A striking modern development is the rise of hybrid regimes that mix democratic forms with authoritarian substance. In what scholars call competitive authoritarianism, rulers hold multiparty elections that are real contests but are systematically tilted, through control of media, selective use of law, harassment of opponents, and manipulation of the state's resources, so that the incumbent almost always wins. Such regimes are not simply flawed democracies; the uneven playing field is the point. They matter because much democratic backsliding produces exactly this outcome, an elected leader who preserves the appearance of democracy while hollowing out its checks.

Authoritarian regimes survive through a combination of tools. Repression deters and punishes dissent, but repression alone is costly and dangerous. So rulers also rely on co-optation, buying the loyalty of elites and key groups with patronage, offices, and economic favors, and on legitimation, cultivating popular support through nationalism, ideology, economic performance, or claims to provide order. A durable dictatorship typically manages all three. A central problem for any autocrat is information: because subordinates fear delivering bad news and citizens hide their true views, rulers can be blindsided, which helps explain why authoritarian collapse often comes as a surprise.

The study of how such regimes fall, through elite splits, economic crisis, mass protest, foreign pressure, or botched succession, and of what replaces them, sometimes democracy, often another autocracy, is among the most policy-relevant work in the field. It underlines a sober lesson: the removal of a dictator does not guarantee democracy, and building durable accountable government is far harder than toppling a regime.

sections.heading: Electoral Systems, Parties, and Representation
sections.body:
How votes are turned into offices is not a technical afterthought but a decision that shapes the whole character of a political system, influencing the number of parties, the kinds of choices voters face, and how faithfully governments reflect public opinion. Political science has mapped these effects closely, and the study of electoral systems is one of its more cumulative successes.

Electoral systems fall into broad families. Plurality or majoritarian systems, such as the first-past-the-post rule used in the United Kingdom, the United States, and India, elect the single candidate with the most votes in each district. They are simple and produce clear local representatives, but they can waste large numbers of votes and hand a party a majority of seats on a minority of votes. Proportional representation systems, common in continental Europe, allocate seats to parties in proportion to their share of the vote, usually across multi-member districts, so that a party winning a fifth of the votes wins roughly a fifth of the seats. Mixed systems combine the two, as in Germany, seeking local representation and overall proportionality together.

These rules have systematic consequences, summarized in what is known as Duverger's law: plurality rules tend to produce two dominant parties, because voters abandon hopeless candidates and small parties are punished, while proportional rules tend to sustain multiparty systems in which many parties win seats. The choice thus shapes whether a country typically has single-party majority governments that are decisive but may exclude much of the electorate, or coalition governments that are broadly representative but require bargaining and can be less stable. There is a genuine trade-off between accountability and representativeness, and no system is best in every respect.

Political parties are the organizations that structure this competition. They recruit and select candidates, aggregate diverse interests into coherent programs, mobilize voters, organize the legislature, and, once in office, form and sustain governments. By offering voters a small number of labeled alternatives, parties make mass democracy workable; a ballot of thousands of unaffiliated individuals would be unintelligible. Parties range from loose, candidate-centered organizations to disciplined, programmatic machines, and party systems, the stable pattern of competition among them, may be two-party, multiparty, or dominant-party.

Underlying all of this is the concept of representation itself, which is more complex than it appears. Hanna Pitkin distinguished acting for constituents from standing for them descriptively, that is, resembling them in identity or background. A representative may act as a delegate, faithfully transmitting constituents' expressed wishes, or as a trustee, exercising independent judgment about their interests. Debates over whether legislatures should mirror the population's composition, and over how to ensure that historically excluded groups are represented, connect these institutional questions to deeper normative ones about what democratic representation is for.

sections.heading: Political Behavior: Voters, Opinion, and Participation
sections.body:
Beyond institutions lies the behavior of ordinary people, and political science devotes a major subfield to how citizens form opinions, decide whether and how to participate, and cast their votes. This work is heavily empirical, built on decades of surveys, experiments, and increasingly on large-scale data, and it has produced findings that often unsettle comfortable assumptions about democratic citizens.

A foundational question is why people vote at all. Rational-choice analysis notes a paradox: since a single vote almost never decides an election, the expected benefit of voting is tiny while the cost, however small, is real, so a purely self-interested calculator might stay home. Yet millions vote. The resolution lies in factors the narrow calculation omits, a sense of civic duty, expressive satisfaction, social pressure, and habit, which experiments confirm can raise turnout. Turnout itself varies widely across countries and groups and is shaped by rules such as registration procedures, compulsory voting, and election timing.

How do voters decide? Several models compete and each captures part of the truth. The sociological model emphasizes stable group memberships, class, religion, region, ethnicity, that anchor loyalties. The party-identification model, developed by scholars at Michigan in the 1950s and 60s, treats a durable psychological attachment to a party, often inherited from one's family, as the central driver, coloring how people interpret everything else. Rational or issue-voting models portray voters as choosing the candidate closest to their own preferences or judging incumbents retrospectively on performance, especially economic performance. In practice most voters blend these, leaning heavily on partisan identity and simple cues because acquiring detailed information is costly.

That reliance on shortcuts connects to a sobering body of research on public opinion. Studies since the 1960s have found that many citizens possess little detailed political knowledge, hold views that are unstable or loosely connected, and are strongly influenced by how questions and choices are framed. Some scholars conclude that voters are dangerously uninformed; others argue that people use reasonable heuristics, cues from trusted parties, groups, and leaders, to reach decisions not far from what fuller information would yield, and that publics in the aggregate can be more rational than individuals. The debate is unresolved and consequential for how much faith to place in direct citizen control.

Participation extends well beyond voting to include contacting officials, joining organizations, donating, protesting, and, increasingly, online activity. Such participation is unequal, tilted toward the wealthier and more educated, which raises concerns that government responds more to some citizens than others. A related concern is affective polarization, the growing tendency in some democracies for partisans to dislike and distrust the opposing side as people, not merely to disagree with them, which strains the mutual tolerance that stable democracy requires. Understanding these patterns is essential to judging how democracy actually functions.

sections.heading: International Relations: Politics Among Nations
sections.body:
International relations studies politics beyond the state, the interactions of states and other actors in a world that, crucially, has no overarching government. This condition of anarchy, meaning the absence of a supreme authority above states rather than chaos, is the field's central premise and the source of its hardest problems. Within a state, a government can enforce agreements and provide security; among states, each must ultimately rely on itself, and this shapes everything from war to trade.

The field is organized around competing theoretical traditions, each a lens rather than a complete truth. Realism holds that states are the main actors, that they pursue power and security in a self-help world, and that conflict is a recurring feature of international life; classical realists trace this to human nature, while structural realists, following Kenneth Waltz, trace it to anarchy itself, which forces even peaceful states to arm and balance against rivals. The balance of power, in which states ally to prevent any one from dominating, is a characteristic realist mechanism. Liberalism counters that cooperation is possible and common: international institutions, economic interdependence through trade, and the spread of democracy can mitigate anarchy's dangers, and the observation that democracies rarely if ever fight one another, the democratic peace, is a much-discussed liberal claim. Constructivism argues that the international system is not fixed by material forces alone but shaped by ideas, identities, and norms; anarchy, in Alexander Wendt's phrase, is what states make of it, and enemies, friends, and rivals are socially constructed roles.

These lenses illuminate the field's core subjects. The study of war and peace asks why states fight, examining causes at the level of individuals and leaders, of states and their regimes, and of the international system, a division of levels of analysis that organizes much research. The security dilemma explains how one state's defensive buildup can frighten others into arming, producing spirals of tension no one wanted. Nuclear weapons introduced the logic of deterrence, in which security rests paradoxically on the credible threat of catastrophic retaliation.

International political economy, a major branch, studies the politics of global trade, finance, and development: who gains and loses from open markets, why states cooperate or clash over economic rules, and how power and wealth interact. Alongside states, the field increasingly attends to other actors, international organizations such as the United Nations, regional bodies such as the European Union, multinational corporations, and transnational networks, and to global problems that no single state can solve, above all climate change, pandemics, and the governance of a connected world economy. Whether such collective challenges can be managed in a system of sovereign states, through institutions, norms, and self-interest rightly understood, is among the defining questions of contemporary international relations, and one on which the field offers analysis rather than guarantees.

sections.heading: Public Policy, Bureaucracy, and Political Economy
sections.body:
Deciding who governs is only half of politics; the other half is what governments actually do, and the study of public policy, administration, and political economy addresses this practical face of the discipline. Public policy is the study of the choices governments make and decline to make, and of the processes by which problems become priorities, options are weighed, decisions are taken, and results follow, or fail to.

Analysts often describe policymaking as a cycle, a simplification that nonetheless organizes the subject. It begins with agenda-setting, the contest over which problems get attention, since countless issues compete and few are addressed; John Kingdon influentially argued that policies change when separate streams of problems, proposals, and politics converge in a window of opportunity. Formulation follows, in which options are devised and analyzed. Adoption is the authoritative choice through legislation or executive action. Implementation, the least glamorous and most decisive stage, is where policy meets the world through the agencies that carry it out. Evaluation asks whether the policy worked, feeding back into future decisions. Real policymaking is messier and more iterative than any cycle suggests, marked by what Charles Lindblom called muddling through, incremental adjustment rather than comprehensive redesign.

Implementation depends on bureaucracy, the permanent professional administration that turns law into action. Max Weber described the modern bureaucracy as an ideal type: hierarchical, rule-bound, staffed by trained officials in defined offices, keeping written records, and applying rules impersonally, a form he saw as technically superior for handling complex tasks at scale. Bureaucracy is indispensable, yet it raises its own political problems. Officials possess expertise and discretion that elected leaders lack, creating a principal-agent problem: how can citizens and their representatives ensure that unelected administrators serve public purposes rather than their own interests or those of the groups they regulate? Concerns about red tape, capture by regulated industries, and unaccountable power are perennial, as are debates over how much discretion frontline officials should exercise.

Political economy analyzes the deep entanglement of states and markets, rejecting the idea that economics and politics can be studied apart. It asks how political choices shape economic outcomes, through property rules, taxation, regulation, and spending, and how economic interests shape political choices. Public choice theory applies the assumption of self-interested rationality to political actors themselves, treating voters, politicians, and bureaucrats as pursuing their own ends, and it highlights problems such as rent-seeking, in which groups lobby for privileges that benefit them at general expense. Debates over the proper size and role of the state, over how to correct market failures such as pollution or monopoly without creating government failures, and over the sources of national prosperity, which recent work ties heavily to the quality of institutions, run through this field and connect the discipline directly to the great practical arguments of public life.

sections.heading: Enduring Debates, Pitfalls, and Connections
sections.body:
Having surveyed the discipline's questions and subfields, it is worth stepping back to name the debates that animate it, the errors it teaches students to avoid, and the wider world of knowledge to which it connects. Political science does not aspire to settle the deepest arguments; part of its value lies in stating them clearly and testing claims that people otherwise assert on faith.

Several tensions run throughout. There is the tension between the empirical and the normative, between explaining how politics works and judging how it should, and the discipline insists on keeping them distinct while acknowledging that facts and values inevitably meet in practice. There is the debate over structure versus agency, whether outcomes are driven by impersonal forces, institutions, economies, geography, or by the choices of individuals and leaders; most careful work grants a role to both. There is disagreement over the weight of institutions versus culture, whether well-designed rules can secure good government anywhere or whether underlying values and social trust are decisive. And there is the abiding question, running from Plato to the present, of the proper balance between liberty and order, between majority rule and minority rights, and between the individual and the collective.

The discipline also trains its students against characteristic pitfalls in reasoning about politics. The first is confusing correlation with causation, seeing that two things go together, such as wealth and democracy, and leaping to conclusions about which causes which, or whether a third factor causes both. The second is selecting on the outcome, studying only successful revolutions or failed states and drawing lessons that vanish once the full range of cases is examined. A third is normative reasoning disguised as description, smuggling one's preferences into supposedly factual claims. A fourth is ethnocentrism, treating one country's arrangements as the natural standard by which all others are judged. Guarding against these is much of what a political science education instills.

Finally, the discipline is deeply connected to its neighbors and to public life. It borrows models from economics and returns questions about power that pure economics neglects; it shares methods and concerns with sociology, psychology, and history; it engages philosophy on justice and law on rules and rights; and it increasingly uses statistics and data science. Its findings inform, and are informed by, the practical work of governing, campaigning, diplomacy, and advocacy. Yet its practitioners are careful to distinguish analysis from activism: understanding how power works is not the same as endorsing any use of it. Studied honestly, political science offers citizens something valuable and increasingly scarce, the capacity to reason clearly about collective life, to recognize the trade-offs that every political arrangement entails, and to hold claims about power to the standard of evidence.
